intro: Body parts you need at the doctor’s, when exercising, and when talking about clothes.
p.la nariz.nota: The /θ/ guide reflects much of Spain; in seseante varieties, z sounds like /s/.
b1.texto:
In ordinary contexts, when it is clear whose body part you mean, Spanish often uses **el, la, los, las** instead of a possessive: **levanta la mano**, **tengo las piernas cansadas**, **me duele la espalda**. A possessive can be used for emphasis or contrast.

**La mano** is feminine: **la mano derecha**, **las manos frías**.

**Derecho** and **izquierdo** agree with the body part: **el pie derecho**, **la mano derecha**, **el brazo izquierdo**, **la pierna izquierda**.

**El dedo** means a finger or a toe; add **de la mano** or **del pie** to specify: **los dedos de la mano**, **los dedos del pie**.
b2.f2: Yes. Now your right hand on your left knee.
b4.o1.refuerzo: Mano is feminine, in spite of the -o.
b5.o0.refuerzo: This means the feet as a whole; dedos can refer to fingers or toes.
b5.o2.refuerzo: Those are the fingers or toes.
b6.o0.refuerzo: With the body, Spanish uses the article.
b6.o1.refuerzo: The article is enough: tengo already says whose.
b10.texto:
**The app cannot check this part.** For the writing, please use pen and paper. For the speaking, say it out loud and, if you can, practise with a native speaker or a teacher who can correct you.

**Write (30–40 words).** Describe an invented monster: how many heads, eyes, arms and legs it has.

**Speak (about 30 seconds).** Give aloud the instructions for a short stretching routine, naming the parts of the body.
